rationale: encapsulated ginger extract and Beck anxiety scores in migraine — The reported day-90 comparison was inconclusive (p = .46) and the registration lists different outcomes. The population had migraine and used an extract.

ginger rhizome powder and Hamilton anxiety with concurrent SSRI use — The publisher abstract explicitly identifies IRCT20201108049306N1 and reports increased active-arm scores while concluding anxiety decreased. The registered powder, SSRIs and Hamilton measures do not resolve the direction without the original tables or a correction.

dried extract plus propranolol and Beck anxiety scores in migraine — The original paper gives a day-90 comparison of 17.2 versus 17.1 points (p = .84). Its registered outcomes list migraine and the published population differs from Parkinson disease.

ginger capsules and dyspepsia quality-of-life subitem — The 51 completers improved on overall dyspepsia quality of life. The separate tension item was inconclusive at p=.670. The report does not supply a Parkinson anxiety endpoint or the registered EQ-5D item results.

oral dried ginger suspension and elevated plus-maze behavior — Both ginger groups spent longer in open arms than the water group in Table 1. Methods conflict on group count and oral dose. This powdered suspension in mice leaves grated ginger and Parkinson anxiety unresolved.

oral aqueous extract of supermarket ginger and rat maze — Open-arm time averaged 30 versus 20 seconds, with no significant open-field crossing difference. Filtered extract and a rat maze cannot identify a clinical effect of eating grated ginger.

anxiety outcomes in a Parkinson formula trial with unresolved ingredients — The official abstract reports Hamilton and self-rated anxiety differences. Publisher metadata identifies legacy PDF record 8908, which was unavailable. Ginger, formula composition and numerical outcomes remain unverified.

ginger extract and mouse dark-box anxiety model — Open-arm time means were greater after extract. The same experiment describes movement differences and gives no extract preparation method, route or dosing duration.

ginger extract and listed MDS-UPDRS Parts I–IV — The scale includes anxious mood but the official record has no separately listed item outcome or posted results. The dosing arms compare two strengths of ginger root extract.
source-context follow-through with preparation or outcome limits — P-862 reviews ginger and weight or fat loss, without a frozen Parkinson endpoint.

original source context with different preparation, outcome, attribution or population — Ginger rhizome occurs in the described multicomponent Banxia houpu formula. No separately assigned grated ginger and anxiety result.

ginger in a four-herb capsule and composite menopause symptoms — Four ingredients changed together. The mental domain was reported in menopause, without a separately measured ginger or Parkinson anxiety effect.
original study or review context for the exposure and endpoint — The current study assigned saffron extract. The earlier four-herb mixture contains ginger and measured composite menopausal symptoms.

original study or review context for the exposure and endpoint — Its preclinical background includes ginger extracts and anxiety-like animal behaviors. No graded or otherwise matched culinary clinical exposure for anxiety.

oral ethanolic rhizome extract and mouse maze behavior — Open-arm occupancy increased at both tested extract doses. The paper reports no significant 60-minute locomotor difference but gives no numerical locomotor values. No fresh grated or clinical Parkinson contrast.

The original abstract reports an artificial membrane assay on seven isolated ginger compounds. The full assay tables remain restricted and the experiment did not measure mental or behavioral outcomes.

four-herb ginger blend and Hamilton anxiety in opioid dependence — The abstract reports favorable time-by-treatment p=.035 for the mixture with only 41 of 81 completing. No estimate specific to ginger or Parkinson disease.

topical fresh ginger juice in a mixed IBS treatment and anxiety-related quality of life — The author abstract reports favorable between-group anxiety-related item scores at days 7 and 28. The plaster contains other herbs and no oral ginger-only arm. Separate tabular results remain open.

intraperitoneal isolated 6-shogaol and anxiety-like behavior after mouse head injury — Open-arm entries increased versus the injured control while ambulation fell in the tables. The Results prose conflicts with both a significance marker and the direction of ambulation. No clinical anxiety or grated ginger exposure was measured.

ginger oral capsules and Spielberger anxiety in burn inpatients — Ginger and placebo had inconclusive visit-level differences through day 6. The report does not specify ginger species or preparation. This cohort was treated for burns.

randomized ginger extract drink and postoperative HARS categories — No-anxiety category 18/20 to 20/20 versus 14/20 to 14/20. The post-only comparison p=.0293 has baseline imbalance and does not supply an adjusted anxiety severity estimate.

standardized ginger root powder and a secondary anxiety outcome in healthy adults — The original manuscript and indexed journal table give DASS-21 anxiety median change −1 versus 0, Mann–Whitney U = 286, p = .511 in the thesis and .51 rounded in the journal. Low baseline scores, a short study, and healthy adults limit the comparison.

standardized ginger root powder and HADS anxiety during chemotherapy — All three reported HADS anxiety differences have confidence intervals crossing zero. The time-by-group test gave p = .352. The protocol included this as a secondary outcome.

inhaled ginger essential oil and nervousness during an acute cognitive stressor — In a crossover of 20 male students, task-time nervousness ratings were 35.0 with ginger aroma and 32.4 with scentless control. Subjective condition comparisons were inconclusive. Selected physiological stress response contrasts favored ginger.

bitter-ginger extract and HADS anxiety in cancer — The uncontrolled study reports improvement with a different Zingiber species. Sixteen of 35 completed eight weeks. Exact anxiety changes and full formulation details remain unavailable.

dietary gingerol-enriched extract and open-field behavior in diabetic rats — Figure 1 reports more center time and entries in extract-treated neuropathy rats. Methods describes eight weeks, while Results references five. Open-field measures and concentrated extract do not resolve culinary ginger and clinical anxiety.

oral gingerol extract and open-field behavior in female rats with nerve ligation — Center entries increased for the higher dose versus ligation vehicle at week four in Figure 2, p < .05. The abstract describes both doses more broadly. Concentrated extract and a pain-model behavior do not establish an effect on Parkinson anxiety.

ginger water extract and stress-model behavior in rats — The experiment measured sucrose drinking, swim immobility, memory tasks and thermal withdrawal. It reports no dedicated anxiety outcome and differs from consumption of grated ginger in Parkinson disease.

oral ginger extract and anxiety-like behavior in a prenatal valproate mouse model — The original abstract describes favorable anxiety-like behavior after four weeks. No numerical result, clinical anxiety scale or fresh culinary exposure is available.

combined standardized ginger and ginkgo extract in rat maze — The combined preparation increased open-arm behavior at a lower dose and decreased approach at a higher dose. The 1 mg/kg finding was inconclusive. The effect of freshly grated ginger alone and clinical anxiety were not assessed.

ginger and ginkgo extract ratios in rat maze — The 2.5:1 mixture at 1 mg/kg increased open-arm behavior. Other ratios gave no detected effect. This experiment does not isolate ginger and differs from the earlier experiment at the same total dose.

single-dose standardized ginger extract drink and postoperative patient-rated anxiety — Supplemental Table 1 gives VAS means of 2.00 vs 1.21 (p = .420) on day one and 1.62 vs 0.71 (p = .266) on day two, n = 24 each. The trial reports no baseline-adjusted anxiety-change contrast. This is the same already catalogued perioperative cohort.
The mouse pharmacokinetic experiment documents brain and serum concentrations after injected isolated 6-gingerol. No anxiety, patient exposure or culinary preparation was tested.

One participant recalled perceived calming after ginger and describes tea with honey or chewing. The second post repeats the account. Preparation, concurrent medication and Parkinson diagnosis remain unclear.
